g.text: SIMULATED DATA
PERSONA CANVAS
Three ways the same job fails
DoseDay core task: take today’s doses on time. Built from 5 interviews (P1–P5), extracted by Claude, then checked line by line against the transcripts.
CAPSTONE 02 · PERSONAS
38 claims checked · 13 changed · 0 invented statistics
The Shifter
“Rowan”, 59 · rotating shift work, employer unnamed · source: P1
3 scheduled + 2 as-needed · age self-corrected
“I’d rather have nothing than something that shames me.”
“Tomorrow’s problem is tomorrow’s.”
P1 · after deleting a good app over one big red circle
WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE
Rotation, no normal day: early 6:15–2:15, middle 2:15–10:15, late
10:15–6:15, then four days off. Up at 4:40, on the floor by 6:15.
Three every morning. Two as-needed: one for a bad back, the other only
“a strong one for the pain” they are not supposed to take every day.
A pill box is the real system, and it has been lost once: a coat pocket,
a friend’s house. A spare with old ones in it lives in the drawer.
Misses cluster after nights: “I would say one or two. Maybe. It’s not
something I count.” The hedge is kept, never converted into a rate.
WHY IT FAILS
The app judged them. One missed night became a verdict:
“I have done everything right for that medication for two years and one screen
tells me I’m a bad patient.”
It assumed a fixed morning and never asked about nights.
It vanished without confirming. Snooze left them unsure whether the dose
was recorded at all: “If something disappears I don’t know about, I can’t trust it.”
ROUTINE AS LIVED
Tick the box by hand before a 6:15 start, in the dark. One app was tried and
deleted; they have never kept one, and do not want to be reminded in a tone.
TRIED AND DROPPED
One app, downloaded by their sister. “A very nice app, I must admit.”
Dropped the morning after the red circle appeared.
DESIGN CONSEQUENCE
No shame states, ever. Reversible check-in, counted once even if pressed
twice. A “you’re on nights tonight” state instead of a lecture. Big targets:
read one-handed, glasses off, at the end of a shift.
Privacy is a choice, not a setting: “It has to be my choice what leaves the phone.”
Their daughter is a nurse, so a daily report would become a row in their house.
ASSUMPTIONS TO TEST — NOT FINDINGS
A1 That a shift-aware schedule is enough for nights. Never tested with them. Method: 5-day shift diary.
A2 That the daughter would accept a chosen weekly summary. That fear is P1’s, not hers. Method: interview her.
GROUNDED 9 · ASSUMPTIONS 2 · 0 stats
P1 only
The Unbothered
“Jay”, 34 · warehouse team lead · source: P2 · gender not stated
2 medications · written gender-neutral on purpose
“I don’t need to be a patient. I need a tap.”
“A streak is a weapon.”
P2 · after three medication apps in four years
WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE
Up at 4:50, on site at 6, runs the safety briefing before the team arrives.
One with the first coffee. One with dinner at half seven.
Weekly box, filled Sunday night, two minutes: “the box has never let me
down and I don’t have to be anywhere near it.”
Morning dose is bulletproof. Evening is not: “the evening one is a coin toss
when I’m late.” Both halves are kept, exactly as spoken.
About thirty apps, two hundred accounts, and no patience for one more sign-up.
WHY IT FAILS
It wanted a diary: “it’s a diary with a push notification attached.” Why is it
interested in my mood? “I’m not here for my mood.”
Sign-up before the first dose. “I have two hundred accounts. I’m not creating
another account to swallow a pill.”
A record becomes a judgement: “a dose log makes me a worse person.” A 40-day streak
was ended on purpose rather than be seen to break.
ROUTINE AS LIVED
Coffee, then the tablet, then the van. The fragile moment is not the morning, it
is 9pm dinner after a double shift and a dose window that has closed.
TRIED AND DROPPED
Three attempts in four years. Two deletions are described in their own words;
the third is simply gone, and the reason was never narrated.
DESIGN CONSEQUENCE
One tap and nothing else. No account, no streak, no badge, no compliance
chart, no morning pep talk. Five seconds is the stated ceiling on any
interaction. “The best version of this product is the one I stop noticing.”
Open question, not a feature: they want no record, while P5 wants a full one.
ASSUMPTIONS TO TEST — NOT FINDINGS
B1 That five seconds is a real ceiling and not a figure of speech. Method: timed tap test,
low-end device, one hand, gloves. B2 No counter-example exists: they keep no log at all.
GROUNDED 8 · ASSUMPTIONS 2 · 0 stats
P2 only
The Unanchored
“Ada”, 67, lives alone · “Ray”, 45, takes fares and deliveries · P3+P4
5 and 3 medications · merged on one shared failure
“A week is a conversation. A day is an accusation.”
“Now, later, or already done. Three states. That’s it.”
P3 and P4 · the merge is a stated decision, not a blend
WHY THEY ARE ONE PERSON
Ada’s bin and whiteboard only work in her kitchen. Ray wakes up in a car park.
Both keep a routine that cannot travel, and both were failed by instructions
written for someone else. Same failure, different materials.
WHY IT FAILS
Nobody told Ada the scale of one missed dose. She carried it for two weeks and
cried in the car: “I had been afraid of my own medicine for two weeks…”
Instructions are written for a clinician. P3: “Take one tablet by mouth.”
By mouth! P4: “Take with food” is two words and five hundred ways to get it wrong.
Small targets fail silently and the blame lands on the finger: “The app never
did it. My finger did it.” Ada lost four typed names and quit that day.
There is nobody to ask. P4: “I can’t ring the pharmacist from a car park. That’s
the actual emotion. The annoyance of having no one to ask.”
No day-of-week tracking: a missed day would sit on Ada’s board forever as a day
she failed. Ray cannot be asked to unlock a phone while driving.
ROUTINE AS LIVED
Ada: two white tablets in the morning, three in the evening. Every day. No days.
Ray: one in the cup holder with the coffee; one needs food he may not get until 11pm.
TRIED AND DROPPED
Ada abandoned a day-of-week box, then an app that lost her typing. Ray has never
used a medication app at all — every claim about him is untested preference.
DESIGN CONSEQUENCE
The system has to survive a missing routine: travel, no kitchen, someone else’s
kitchen. One sentence per medication — what it is for, what to watch, what a single
miss means. Big targets, dead space to be wrong in, and no tone whatsoever.
Sharing is weekly, chosen, and announced: a week is a conversation.
ASSUMPTIONS TO TEST — NOT FINDINGS
C1 That one travelling routine suits both. They were merged on one shared failure and
never tested together. Method: travel scenario test with each, separately.
BOUNDARIES HELD IN VERIFICATION
Ada names no medication and declines to name her eye condition: no diagnosis is added.
Ray’s urgent-care visit and his kidney stone are separate events. He was not admitted.
GROUNDED 11 · ASSUMPTIONS 2 · 0 stats
P3+P4 composite
P5 — “The Audit Trail”: the critic, kept beside the personas
29, reads privacy policies, has a working system, and refused every product in this research. Not a persona: a persona would flatter them.
“I will not make the two hundred and first to swallow a pill.”
P5 · the only participant with a working system who has never put medication in an app
THEIR THREE OBJECTIONS, WHICH THE PACK MUST ANSWER
1. The routine that does not travel. “The box is only correct in my kitchen… Wednesday is a lie.”
2. Onboarding that asks what they already know. “Tell me something I don’t know.”
3. Privacy with a line in it: the fact may be shared, the meaning may not. Anxiety, not depression.
They also hand this pack its thesis, and it is the reason this page is not three tidy cards:
“The design question isn’t how do we get her to take the pill, it’s how does the system behave
when the routine is gone.”
Verified, not generated
Every claim on this page was checked against the transcripts by hand.
rejected outright
corrected
annotated
confirmed unchanged
WHAT THE MODEL GOT WRONG
1. Invented an industry. “Hospital-adjacent” is in no transcript: specific, plausible, untraceable.
2. Claimed no participant states their gender. Two of five say it plainly. A hedge is not a truth.
3. Labelled a stage “anxious” against the participant’s own “It’s not fear.”
4. Replaced nuance with a motive: “surveillance, not care” against “is she wrong to ask? No.”
5. Flagged a contradiction, then shipped the merge that hid it. Flagging is not resolving.
6. Spliced two separate answers into one flowing quote. Caught by the model, on request.
OURS, NOT THE MODEL’S: “shift supervisor”, “distribution centre”, “retired” and “PhD student” came from our
own filenames. Four unsourced claims survived verification. Fixed as defect C-05.
Personas are composites written for design use. First names are fictional and carry no evidence about gender: P1, P2 and P5 never state theirs, so they are written neutral.
Simulated corpus: no human was interviewed. Every behavioural claim is a quotation or a labelled assumption; no adherence rate or diagnosis is added anywhere.
